name: Nebuchadnezzar II
info: Nebuchadnezzar II was the second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling from 605 to 562 BCE; he destroyed Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah in 587 BCE and rebuilt the city of Babylon.

facts.born: Year of birth not known; the dates 605 to 562 BCE are those of his reign. Eldest son of Nabopolassar, founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire
facts.died: 562 BCE at Babylon, after an illness; the last tablet dated to his reign and the first of his successor Amel-Marduk both bear 7 October
facts.role: High priest of the Eanna temple in Uruk (attested 626/625 to 617 BCE); crown prince and army commander under his father; king of Babylon from 605 to 562 BCE
facts.known: the victory over Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BCE; the destruction of Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah in 587 BCE and the Babylonian captivity; the campaigns against Tyre; the rebuilding of Babylon, including the Ishtar Gate, the Esagila and the Etemenanki; the failed invasion of Egypt; his portrayal in the Bible

t: As crown prince Nebuchadnezzar commanded the Babylonian army that crushed an Egyptian force at Carchemish in 605 BCE, and became king within weeks when his father Nabopolassar died.
His early reign saw a failed invasion of Egypt and the unrest that followed it, and in 587 BCE he destroyed Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah and deported many of its people to Babylonia.

His own inscriptions deal mainly with building, and he rebuilt Babylon on a large scale; the Bible and later writers made him a figure of hostile memory, though the Book of Daniel blends his story with that of a later king.
dyk: Nebuchadnezzar's name, Nabû-kudurri-uṣur, was read in earlier scholarship as "Nabu, protect the boundary", but modern historians support the meaning "Nabu, watch over my heir".
ev: Nebuchadnezzar is first attested as high priest of the Eanna temple in Uruk, a post he is recorded in until 617 BCE
He commands the Babylonian army at Carchemish and defeats the Egyptians under Necho II; on his father's death he returns to Babylon and is proclaimed king
He invades Egypt; the Babylonian Chronicle records heavy losses on both sides and the invasion fails
He takes Jerusalem, captures King Jeconiah and installs Zedekiah as king of Judah
After Zedekiah's revolt he destroys Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah, and the Jews are deported to Babylonia
The land city of Tyre is taken after a siege, while the island part of the city is left alone
A fragmentary inscription suggests a further campaign against Egypt under Amasis II, which did not bring Egypt under Babylonian rule
Nebuchadnezzar dies at Babylon after a reign of 43 years and Amel-Marduk succeeds him

sections.early:
Nebuchadnezzar was the eldest son of Nabopolassar, who founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire by rebelling against Assyria. His inscriptions call him his father's "first" or "chief son" and "legitimate heir". His year of birth is not known. His Akkadian name, Nabû-kudurri-uṣur, means "Nabu, watch over my heir", and it matched that of Nebuchadnezzar I, a warrior-king who had ruled Babylon more than five centuries earlier. Nabopolassar's own origin is unclear: historians have called him a Chaldean, an Assyrian or a Babylonian, although the term "Chaldean dynasty" is still widely used for his family.

Nabopolassar seems to have been closely tied to Uruk, and Nebuchadnezzar's daughters lived there. In 2007 Michael Jursa proposed that Nabopolassar belonged to a prominent Uruk family, and that a governor of Uruk named Kudurru, whose body the Assyrians dragged through the streets because of his sons' anti-Assyrian activity, was Nebuchadnezzar's grandfather. Nebuchadnezzar himself is attested from 626/625 to 617 BCE as high priest of the Eanna temple in Uruk, under the nickname "Kudurru", which would have made him very young. The empire that rose in Assyria's place was powerful but hastily built and politically unstable.
sections.rise:
Little survives of Nebuchadnezzar's military career before he was king. A letter to the Eanna temple suggests that he took part in his father's campaign against Harran in 610 BCE, where the remnant of the Assyrian state under Ashur-uballit II had gathered. The defeat of Ashur-uballit in 609 BCE ended the ancient Assyrian monarchy. According to the Babylonian Chronicles, Nebuchadnezzar also commanded an army in a mountainous region for several months in 607 BCE.

After Harran fell, Pharaoh Necho II led an Egyptian army into the former Assyrian lands to try to restore Assyria as a buffer state, and the Egyptians took the Levant largely unopposed as far as Carchemish. In 605 BCE Nebuchadnezzar, as sole commander because his father stayed in Babylon, perhaps through illness, crossed the Euphrates at Carchemish and defeated them. The Babylonian Chronicle says that a single Egyptian did not return home, and that Nebuchadnezzar conquered all of Hamath.

Nabopolassar died a few weeks later. The news reached Nebuchadnezzar on 8 Abu (late July) while he was still in the field, and he arranged matters with the Egyptians and hurried to Babylon, where he was proclaimed king on 1 Ulūlu (mid-August). His haste may have reflected a danger that a brother, Nabu-shum-lishir, whom Nabopolassar had called "his equal brother", would claim the throne. No usurper appeared at this time.
sections.deeds:
After burying his father in a palace in Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar went back to Syria. The Babylonian Chronicle, which survives for his first eleven years, records that in 604 BCE he took Ascalon, whose king was captured and taken to Babylon and whose city was plundered and levelled; modern excavations confirm the city was largely destroyed. In 598 BCE he marched on the Kingdom of Judah, whose king Jehoiakim had begun to defy Babylon by 601 BCE. Jehoiakim died during the siege and his son Jeconiah was captured. The Chronicle says the city fell on the second of Addaru in 597 BCE and that Nebuchadnezzar installed a king of his choice, Jeconiah's uncle Zedekiah.

In 589 BCE Zedekiah refused tribute, and Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah in 587 BCE, an event that ended Judah and began the Babylonian captivity. Excavations show that Jerusalem and its surroundings were destroyed and depopulated. Tyre had rebelled at about the same time; its land city was taken in 571 BCE, and the island city, which could not be taken without naval support, came to terms and kept vassal kings under heavier Babylonian control.

Most of Nebuchadnezzar's inscriptions concern building. He rebuilt Babylon, restored the Esagila, completed the Etemenanki ziggurat, restored the South Palace, built a North Palace and a Summer Palace, and rebuilt the Processional Street and the Ishtar Gate, faced with blue and yellow glazed bricks. He also built the Median Wall, dug the Nar-Shamash canal and began the Royal Canal.
sections.opponents:
The first years of the reign were poor. Nebuchadnezzar invaded Egypt in 601 BCE, and the Babylonian Chronicle records that both armies suffered a huge number of casualties. The invasion failed. His poor record had dangerous results: in 595 BCE he had to put down a rebellion in Babylon itself, a man was tried before him for breaking his oath to the king in 594 BCE, and the Bible says that the kings of Ammon, Edom, Moab, Sidon and Tyre met in Jerusalem to consider throwing off Babylonian control. The Assyriologist Israel Ephʿal wrote that Babylon was seen by its contemporaries more as a "paper tiger" than as a great empire.

The people of Judah bore the cost of the later campaigns. Jeconiah was taken to Babylon, and the destruction of 587 BCE led to the deportation of the Jews to Babylonia. According to the Bible and the historian Josephus, Zedekiah was captured at Jericho, taken to Riblah, made to watch his sons executed and then blinded and imprisoned in Babylon. No cuneiform source describes the fall of Judah, so the biblical account is the only known one. The intensity of the destruction in the Levant may have come from something akin to a scorched earth policy aimed at keeping Egypt from gaining a foothold.

His military record has been judged unevenly. His military achievements can be questioned, since the borders of his empire had not noticeably grown by the end of his reign and he had not conquered Egypt. Josephus's account, in which he invades Egypt five years after Jerusalem and appoints a new pharaoh, is not entirely historical.
sections.last:
A stele from Tahpanhes uncovered in 2011 records that he tried to invade Egypt in 582 BCE and that Apries' forces repelled him. A fragmentary Babylonian inscription, BM 33041, of 568 to 567 BCE mentions Egypt and possibly Amasis II, and a fragmentary stele of Amasis may describe a combined attack by land and sea. Recent evidence suggests that the Babylonians gained a foothold in Egypt before Amasis' forces drove them out. Nebuchadnezzar died at Babylon in 562 BCE after reigning 43 years, the longest reign of his dynasty.

The succession was troubled. Amel-Marduk, who had been named crown prince, was not the eldest surviving son: Marduk-nadin-ahi was still alive in 563 BCE, and the reason for the choice is not known. One fragmentary text describes both father and son as parties to a conspiracy and accuses one of them of exploiting Babylon's people and desecrating its temples, and Amel-Marduk seems at one point to have been imprisoned by his father, possibly after Babylonian aristocrats proclaimed him king while Nebuchadnezzar was away. Nebuchadnezzar may have meant to replace him as heir but died first. Amel-Marduk ruled two years before his brother-in-law Neriglissar murdered him and took the throne.
sections.legacy:
Historians have judged Nebuchadnezzar differently as the evidence changed. Because only one of some fifty known inscriptions deals with military action, scholars such as Wolfram von Soden in 1954 took him mainly for a builder. Donald Wiseman's publication of the Babylonian Chronicle in 1956 led historians to see him instead as a warrior. Josette Elayi wrote in 2018 that he was a conqueror, "even though reservations can be had about his military capabilities", and a great builder, adding that little more is known because the sources say little about his personality. He is usually regarded as the greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and he was remembered favourably by the Babylonians.

In Jewish and biblical tradition he is the king who destroyed Jerusalem. The Book of Jeremiah calls him a "lion" and a "destroyer of nations", yet three times also "my servant", an epithet missing from the Septuagint, which some scholars take as a later addition. The Book of Daniel, which scholars widely consider historical fiction, makes him a despotic ruler who goes mad for seven years. Because Daniel calls him the father of Belshazzar, the story of his madness was probably based on Belshazzar's actual father, Nabonidus, the last Neo-Babylonian king.

Later writers confused him with other rulers. Al-Ṭabarī credited him with conquering Egypt, which the historical Nebuchadnezzar never did. Tradition holds that he built the Hanging Gardens of Babylon for his wife Amytis; no archaeological evidence for the gardens has been found.

summary: Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605 to 562 BCE) defeated Egypt at Carchemish as crown prince, then ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire for 43 years. He destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE, failed to conquer Egypt, and rebuilt Babylon, and the Bible made him a figure of hostile memory.
references: Paul-Alain Beaulieu, A History of Babylon, 2200 BC - AD 75 (Wiley, 2018)
Oled Lipschits, The Fall and Rise of Jerusalem: Judah under Babylonian Rule (Eisenbrauns, 2005)
Ronald H. Sack, Images of Nebuchadnezzar: The Emergence of a Legend (Susquehanna University Press, 2004)
Donald J. Wiseman, Nebuchadrezzar and Babylon: The Schweich Letters (Oxford University Press, 1983)
notes: Birth year is not in the article: start -605 is the accession (guide rule), circa true. The article also dates his priesthood at Uruk from 626/625 BCE, so he was alive well before 605.
Death date: the article gives 562 BCE and the shared date of 7 October for the last tablet of his reign and the first of Amel-Marduk's.

Jerusalem: the article gives 598-597 BCE for the first assault, capture on 2 Addaru (early 597); the destruction in 587 BCE, 'probably ended in the summer of 587'. Only the biblical account (and Josephus) covers 587; stated so. Siege length 18-30 months (Books of Kings) left out.

Tyre: Josephus's 13-year siege is debated; the article says Babylon took the land city in 571 BCE, which is used with the island left alone. The article's own section is partly contradictory about the siege's start; the start and length are left out.
Egypt 582 BCE (Tahpanhes stele) and 568-567 BCE (BM 33041, Amasis stele) are tentative in the article; the 568 event uses the article's hedge. The label year 568 is the start of '568-567'.

The article names Cyaxares's daughter Amytis from Berossus but also notes Ctesias's different version; the wife is mentioned only in the Hanging Gardens line, kept as tradition. Her parentage was left out.

Left out: his six sons and three daughters by name, the Median alliance, the 603 BCE campaign (Gaza or Kummuh, speculative), Nabu-shum-lishir's possible revolt (speculative), the Moabite city destruction, the titles and name-etymology details beyond the dyk, and the Belshazzar/Nitocris material.
Legacy section: the Daniel/Nabonidus sentence rests on the article's 'probable' and is not attributed to a named scholar; the editor may want to attribute it to historians.
Not in the article, so not used: the Hanging Gardens' later fame beyond the tradition; Nabucco and Blake (listed only under See also).
